name: A <TT>Context</TT> class must support two versions of an algorithm. Two simple options are a parameter (<TT>compute(strategy)</TT>) or separate methods (<TT>computeWithStrategyA()</TT>, <TT>computeWithStrategyB()</TT>). A third option makes Context abstract with subclasses <TT>ContextImplA</TT> and <TT>ContextImplB</TT>. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: With a parameter or separate methods, clients choose the strategy, which is a feature, but a new strategy means changing the existing class.
answers.comment: L6, slide 3: The choice by clients is not a drawback, but extending the class violates the open-closed principle.

answers.body: Subclassing the context tackles the open-closed issue, but changing the behavior requires redirecting all clients to a new instance.
answers.comment: L6, slide 4: Inheritance helps with extension, but an existing context object cannot change its subclass.

answers.body: With a parameter or separate methods, a new strategy can be added without touching Context, so the open-closed principle holds.
answers.comment: L6, slide 3: Implementing a new strategy requires changes in the existing class.

answers.body: Subclassing the context lets one existing context object switch its behavior at run time without affecting clients.
answers.comment: L6, slide 4: The clients would have to be redirected to the instance of the other subclass.

answers.body: With a parameter, the context itself decides which strategy runs, so clients take no part in the choice.
answers.comment: L6, slide 3: The clients are responsible for choosing the strategy by passing the parameter.

name: Which statements about the structure and collaboration of the Strategy pattern are correct?

answers.body: Context aggregates exactly one Strategy and calls its <TT>algorithmInterface()</TT> from <TT>contextInterface()</TT>.
answers.comment: L6, slide 5: The context delegates the algorithm to the strategy object it holds; the concrete strategies implement the common interface.

answers.body: A client that understands the strategies can pass one to the context (<TT>setStrategy</TT>); another client just calls <TT>contextInterface()</TT>.
answers.comment: L6, slides 5-6: The client that understands the strategies can differ from the client calling the context.

answers.body: Context is abstract, with subclasses <TT>ContextImplA</TT> and <TT>ContextImplB</TT> that override <TT>contextInterface()</TT> for each algorithm.
answers.comment: L6, slide 4: That is the alternative of subclassing the context, which Strategy replaces.

answers.body: Context inherits from Strategy, so it switches algorithms by changing its own class at run time.
answers.comment: L6, slide 5: The context holds a strategy object; changing the algorithm means exchanging that object.

answers.body: Each ConcreteStrategy declares its own interface; every algorithm needs different operations.
answers.comment: L6, slide 5: The concrete strategies implement the common Strategy interface, so the context can use them interchangeably.

name: Which are applicability conditions or consequences of the Strategy pattern?

answers.body: A class with many conditional behaviors can move each branch into its own Strategy class and drop the switch-case.
answers.comment: L6, slide 6: Strategies eliminate conditional statements.

answers.body: The Strategy interface can become more complex, since the strategy has only limited access to the context state.
answers.comment: L6, slide 6: The strategy should be independent of the context, which costs some communication (overhead).

answers.body: Strategy decreases the number of objects in the system. An algorithm no longer needs an object of its own.
answers.comment: L6, slide 6: It increases the number of objects, which is a feature rather than a drawback.

answers.body: Strategies may read all internal fields of the context freely, so Strategy adds no communication overhead.
answers.comment: L6, slide 6: The strategy has limited access to the context state, which causes the overhead.

answers.body: Strategy makes clients simpler. Clients no longer need to know how the individual strategies differ.
answers.comment: L6, slide 6: A client that understands how strategies differ is still needed, though it can differ from the client calling the context.

name: Atoms of a molecule "shake": their positions differ in each frame of a simulation. Two storage approaches exist: all positions in memory (an array), or a buffer holding only a window of frames loaded from a file on demand. Initially they are subclasses <TT>HugeMemAtom</TT> and <TT>BufferedAtom</TT> of <TT>Atom</TT>. Refactoring to Strategy (Atom with an <TT>AtomPositionStrategy</TT>: <TT>AllInMemStrategy</TT> or <TT>BufferedStrategy</TT>) is considered. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: Refactoring pays off only if the storage strategy should change during an atom's lifetime; if it never changes, Strategy is useless here.
answers.comment: L6, slide 9: The design decision depends on whether the strategy changes during the atom's lifetime.

answers.body: With Strategy, each atom can have its own storage strategy and change it at run time while clients keep the same Atom object.
answers.comment: L6, slides 10, 41: The strategy can differ for individual atoms and can change at run time.

answers.body: Strategy is needed whenever two storage variants exist, even if an atom never switches its storage during its lifetime.
answers.comment: L6, slide 9: If the strategy never changes during the lifetime, the Strategy pattern is useless.

answers.body: HugeMemAtom and BufferedAtom cannot share the signature <TT>getPosition(frame)</TT>, so only a strategy hierarchy can unify them.
answers.comment: L6, slide 8: Both subclasses already implement the common getPosition(frame) interface of Atom.

answers.body: With Strategy, all atoms of a residue have to share one storage strategy object, which keeps the memory use low.
answers.comment: L6, slide 10: Every atom can have its own strategy.

name: Which statements about the State pattern are correct?

answers.body: The Context delegates every state-specific request to the current ConcreteState and may pass itself as an argument, so the state can use the context.
answers.comment: L6, slide 14: The context is the primary interface and hands requests to its state object.

answers.body: Either the Context or the ConcreteState subclasses can decide which state succeeds another and under what circumstances.
answers.comment: L6, slide 14: Both variants of controlling transitions are allowed.

answers.body: After the initial configuration, clients have to call the State objects directly and bypass the Context.
answers.comment: L6, slide 14: The Context is the primary interface; clients do not deal with State objects directly.

answers.body: State transitions stay implicit, hidden inside one large conditional of the Context, which is the main benefit of the pattern.
answers.comment: L6, slide 15: State makes transitions explicit and removes large multipart conditionals.

answers.body: State objects can never be shared between contexts. Each one stores the data of exactly one context.
answers.comment: L6, slide 15: State objects can be shared (see the Flyweight pattern).

name: A <TT>Printer</TT> has the operation <TT>print(Document)</TT> and behaves differently when it is Ready, Printing or OutOfToner. Which statements about a design following the State pattern are correct?

answers.body: Printer holds a <TT>PrinterState</TT> reference; <TT>Ready</TT>, <TT>Printing</TT> and <TT>OutOfToner</TT> implement <TT>handle(Document)</TT> and <TT>print()</TT> delegates to the current state.
answers.comment: L6, slides 13-14: The context delegates state-specific requests to the current state object.

answers.body: The transition, for example from Printing to OutOfToner, can be decided by the Printer or by any of the state objects themselves.
answers.comment: L6, slide 14: Either the context or the state subclasses decide the successor state.

answers.body: <TT>Printer.print()</TT> contains one large switch over a status attribute with a branch for Ready, Printing and OutOfToner, each handled inline.
answers.comment: L6, slide 15: Large multipart conditionals depending on state are exactly what State replaces.

answers.body: Clients create a new Printer subclass instance (ReadyPrinter, PrintingPrinter, ...) whenever the status changes and redirect their references to it.
answers.comment: L6, slides 4, 14: Replacing instances forces clients to be redirected; State keeps one Context object.

answers.body: Each Document object stores the printer status and decides by itself how it will be printed on the printer.
answers.comment: L6, slide 14: State-specific behavior belongs to the state objects that the Context delegates to.

name: How does the State pattern differ from the Strategy pattern?

answers.body: A state may keep a reference to its context and replace itself by another state, which a strategy never does.
answers.comment: L6, slide 18: States can store the context and change the context's state; strategies do not.

answers.body: A strategy handles one specific task, whereas states provide the implementation for almost everything the context does.
answers.comment: L6, slide 18: This is the difference in scope of responsibility.

answers.body: Strategies are created by the context itself, while states are passed to the context by clients as parameters.
answers.comment: L6, slide 18: It is the other way round: strategies come in as parameters, states are created by the context.

answers.body: Their class diagrams differ clearly, so the two patterns can be told apart visually without knowing their purpose.
answers.comment: L6, slides 13, 7: State is visually similar to Strategy and has a similar purpose.

answers.body: A strategy changes the strategy of its context when its task is finished, just as a state changes the state.
answers.comment: L6, slide 18: Strategies are not allowed to replace themselves; states are.

name: In the shaking-molecule model, the storage of atom positions could switch between all-in-memory and buffered depending on available memory. There are clear states (enough memory, running out of memory) driving the behavior. Which statements about the decision between State and Strategy are correct?

answers.body: The state-change logic would have to live in every single atom, which wastes memory for the many atoms of a molecule.
answers.comment: L6, slide 16: Putting the transition logic in each atom is a waste of memory.

answers.body: Decentralized knowledge does not work: an atom would switch its storage only when it is called, which can be too late.
answers.comment: L6, slide 16: The storage must change before the atom is asked for its position.

answers.body: State is the better choice. Every atom needs its own memory check to decide when to switch its storage.
answers.comment: L6, slide 16: A per-atom check is exactly what is rejected; a centralized memory manager switches the strategies.

answers.body: State cannot be used when an object has only two states, so a Strategy with two variants is the only option.
answers.comment: L6, slide 16: The reason is where the state-change logic lives, not the number of states.

name: Which statements about the Adapter pattern are correct?

answers.body: An adapter (wrapper) integrates an existing external class by converting its interface into the one our abstraction expects.
answers.comment: L6, slide 20: It converts the interface to a compatible form, like a power plug adapter.

answers.body: An object adapter implements <TT>request()</TT> by re-sending it to an associated adaptee object, e.g. <TT>adaptee.specificRequest()</TT>.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: Object adapter adapts by re-sending to the associated adaptee.

answers.body: An adapter adds new responsibilities to an object while keeping its interface unchanged, so clients are unaffected.
answers.comment: L6, slide 38: That describes Decorator; an adapter gives an object a completely new interface.

answers.body: An adapter hides a complex subsystem behind a simplified, aggregated interface so that clients call fewer operations.
answers.comment: L5, slide 12: That describes Facade; an adapter converts one interface into another and does not simplify a subsystem.

answers.body: A class adapter implements <TT>request()</TT> by re-sending it to a separate adaptee object, whereas an object adapter inherits from the adaptee.
answers.comment: L6, slides 21-22: It is the other way round: class adapter uses multiple inheritance, object adapter uses association.

name:
interface Shape { void display(int x, int y, int w, int h); }  // (x, y) top-left corner, w width, h height
class LegacyRectangle { void show(int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2) { ... } }  // two opposite corners
Drawing code uses Shape. The class LegacyRectangle may not be changed. We write an object adapter Rectangle implements Shape. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: <TT>display(x, y, w, h)</TT> calls <TT>legacy.show(x, y, x + w, y + h)</TT>: the adapter converts width and height into the opposite corner and re-sends the request.
answers.comment: L6, slides 20, 22: Interface conversion plus re-sending to the adaptee; the corner arithmetic is derived, not slide text.

answers.body: <TT>Rectangle</TT> holds a <TT>LegacyRectangle</TT> as an attribute, so clients always keep using <TT>Shape</TT> and the legacy class stays unchanged.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: An object adapter refers to the adaptee and implements the target interface.

answers.body: <TT>display(x, y, w, h)</TT> calls <TT>legacy.show(x, y, w, h)</TT>. Both operations take four numbers in the same order.
answers.comment: L6, slides 20, 22: show() expects the second corner, not the width and height, so the call would draw a wrong rectangle.

answers.body: Change <TT>LegacyRectangle.show()</TT> so that it accepts (x, y, w, h) and the adapter becomes unnecessary. Adapters are for classes we may modify.
answers.comment: L6, slides 20, 23: An adapter is used exactly when an existing class does not match and we integrate it without changing it.

answers.body: Make <TT>Shape</TT> inherit from <TT>LegacyRectangle</TT>, so every shape gets <TT>show()</TT> and the adapter is obsolete.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: Our abstraction stays as it is; the adapter bridges to the adaptee instead.

name: Compare the class adapter and the object adapter. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: One object adapter works with the Adaptee and all its subclasses, whereas a class adapter commits to one concrete Adaptee class.
answers.comment: L6, slides 23-25: The class adapter does not work when a class and all its subclasses are to be adapted.

answers.body: A class adapter is a subclass of the Adaptee, so it can override some of the Adaptee's behavior.
answers.comment: L6, slide 24: This possibility is much more limited in an object adapter.

answers.body: A class adapter needs two objects and an extra pointer indirection to reach the adaptee, unlike an object adapter.
answers.comment: L6, slide 24: A class adapter introduces only one object and needs no additional pointer indirection.

answers.body: Overriding the Adaptee's behavior is easiest with an object adapter.
answers.comment: L6, slide 25: It is harder with an object adapter; it requires subclassing the Adaptee and referring to that subclass.

answers.body: Only a class adapter can adapt several existing subclasses at once through the interface of their common parent class.
answers.comment: L6, slide 23: That is the applicability of the object adapter only.

name: Each TV model is programmed for each kind of remote controller (push-button, touch), so every new TV model or controller multiplies the classes. Which statements describe the Bridge solution?

answers.body: The remote controller (abstraction) holds a reference <TT>imp</TT> to the TV (implementor) and delegates <TT>operation()</TT> to <TT>imp.operationImp()</TT>.
answers.comment: L6, slides 28-29: The abstraction is separated from the implementation and linked by a reference.

answers.body: Both hierarchies can be extended independently by subclassing, so a new TV model needs no new controller classes for any controller.
answers.comment: L6, slide 30: Bridge lets you combine abstractions and implementations and extend them independently.

answers.body: The implementor interface has to be identical to the generic interface of the abstraction.
answers.comment: L6, slide 28: The remote-control interface of the TV can differ from the controller's generic interface, e.g. be lower-level.

answers.body: Bridge needs one subclass for every combination of controller and TV model, so that each pair is programmed separately.
answers.comment: L6, slides 27, 30: That proliferation of classes is the problem Bridge removes.

answers.body: Refined abstractions such as the touch controller replace the implementor, so a controller has to know which TV model it controls.
answers.comment: L6, slide 28: The refined abstractions extend the abstraction's interface; the implementor hierarchy of TV models stays separate.

name: Which are applicability conditions or consequences of the Bridge pattern?

answers.body: Bridge fits when a proliferation of classes shows that an object should be split into two parts, abstraction and implementation.
answers.comment: L6, slide 30: Such a class hierarchy indicates the need for splitting an object into two parts.

answers.body: It decouples interface from implementation, hides implementation details from clients, and changes need not force recompiling client code.
answers.comment: L6, slide 30: These are the listed consequences and applicability conditions.

answers.body: Bridge is the best choice whenever the only goal is to change behavior at run time. No other pattern is needed.
answers.comment: L6, slide 30: If the only reason is a run-time change of behavior, use Strategy instead.

answers.body: Bridge merges abstraction and implementation into one class hierarchy, which reduces the number of classes.
answers.comment: L6, slide 29: Bridge separates the abstraction from the implementation into two hierarchies.

answers.body: Bridge binds an abstraction permanently to one implementation at compile time, which is why clients stay unaffected by changes.
answers.comment: L6, slide 30: Bridge avoids a permanent binding; the implementation can be selected or switched at run time.

name: <TT>java.io.InputStreamReader(InputStream)</TT> creates a character Reader from a binary InputStream and is described as a bridge from byte streams to character streams, although it could also be read as an adapter. The two patterns can lead to similar class diagrams. Which statements about choosing between them are correct?

answers.body: If the problem is a proliferation of classes (e.g. every TV model programmed for each remote controller), I would choose Bridge.
answers.comment: L6, slides 27, 32: Splitting an object into two hierarchies is the Bridge circumstance.

answers.body: If the problem is integrating an existing class hierarchy into another one, I would choose an object adapter.
answers.comment: L6, slide 32: Integrating one hierarchy into another is the Adapter circumstance.

answers.body: The two patterns are interchangeable and the circumstances of the design play no role.
answers.comment: L6, slide 32: The difference lies in the circumstances under which we select the pattern.

answers.body: InputStreamReader is a Decorator. It wraps another stream and therefore keeps the interface of InputStream.
answers.comment: L6, slides 32, 38: A decorator keeps the interface; InputStreamReader turns an InputStream into a Reader, a different interface.

answers.body: Bridge and Adapter differ in that only Bridge needs an association between two classes. An adapter works by inheritance alone.
answers.comment: L6, slides 22, 28: An object adapter also uses an association to the adaptee; the patterns differ in their purpose.

name: A pizza menu offers a base pizza and the toppings sausage, cheese and spinach in any combination. Modeling each combination as a subclass (<TT>PizzaWithSausage</TT>, <TT>PizzaWithCheese</TT>, <TT>PizzaWithSausageAndCheese</TT>, ...) quickly explodes. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: Subclassing needs a class for every non-empty combination: \(2^n - 1\) for \(n\) toppings, e.g. \(2^3 - 1 = 7\).
answers.comment: L6, slides 33, 35: An explosion of subclasses supports every combination (the count is derived).

answers.body: Decorator needs one base class plus one decorator per topping: sausage wraps cheese wraps the pizza, built per order at run time.
answers.comment: L6, slides 34-35: Responsibilities are attached to individual objects dynamically.

answers.body: With Decorator, the toppings must be fixed when the Pizza class is compiled, so a pizza cannot get another topping later.
answers.comment: L6, slides 34, 36: Responsibilities are attached dynamically and can be withdrawn.

answers.body: A Decorator holds a list of components and forwards the call to all of them, like a Composite with many children.
answers.comment: L6, slide 35: A decorator holds exactly one component; that is an important difference from Composite.

answers.body: With Decorator, a pizza with cheese and sausage is one object of a class combining both toppings, created in advance.
answers.comment: L6, slides 33-35: Decorator avoids the combination classes by wrapping objects at run time.

name: Which statements about the structure of the Decorator pattern are correct?

answers.body: Decorator inherits from Component and holds exactly one component; <TT>operation()</TT> forwards to it and a concrete decorator may add behavior.
answers.comment: L6, slide 35: The decorator wraps a component and adds responsibilities before or after forwarding.

answers.body: Decorators can appear anywhere a Component can, so they can wrap other decorators, and they are free to add own operations.
answers.comment: L6, slide 35: This is the important aspect of the pattern.

answers.body: A decorator keeps a list of children and forwards the operation to all of them, which is its main purpose.
answers.comment: L6, slide 35: That is Composite; a decorator wraps exactly one component.

answers.body: A decorator changes the interface of the wrapped component, so clients need different calls for decorated objects.
answers.comment: L6, slide 38: A decorator changes or extends responsibilities, not the interface; an adapter gives a new interface.

answers.body: Concrete decorators must not add operations of their own; that would violate the Component interface.
answers.comment: L6, slide 35: Decorator subclasses are free to add operations for specific functionality.

name: Which are applicability conditions or consequences (including liabilities) of the Decorator pattern?

answers.body: Use it to add responsibilities to individual objects dynamically and transparently, without affecting any other object, for responsibilities that can be withdrawn.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: These are the stated applicability conditions.

answers.body: Liabilities: a decorator and its component are not identical objects, and the design creates lots of little objects.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: Both are listed as liabilities.

answers.body: It offers less flexibility than static inheritance. Decorators are fixed at compile time and cannot be removed.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: It offers more flexibility than static inheritance.

answers.body: Feature-laden classes high in the hierarchy are an advantage. Every feature is available in the base class.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: Decorator avoids feature-laden classes; a simple class gets functionality incrementally.

answers.body: Decorating one object also changes the behavior of all other objects of the same class. The responsibility is added to the class.
answers.comment: L6, slides 34, 36: Responsibilities are added to individual objects without affecting other objects.

name: How is Decorator related to Adapter, Composite and Strategy?

answers.body: A decorator changes or extends an object's responsibilities, not its interface, whereas an adapter gives an object a completely new interface.
answers.comment: L6, slide 38: This separates Decorator from Adapter.

answers.body: A decorator changes the skin of an object, a strategy changes its guts; strategies rather change behavior, decorators rather extend it.
answers.comment: L6, slide 38: These are two alternative ways of changing an object.

answers.body: A decorator's main purpose is to aggregate objects, which makes it a composite with exactly one child that is meant for aggregation.
answers.comment: L6, slide 38: A decorator can be viewed as a degenerate composite, but it adds responsibilities; change is not intended for object aggregation.

answers.body: A decorator changes the guts of an object, while a strategy changes its skin, so both are alternatives to subclassing.
answers.comment: L6, slide 38: The skin and guts are swapped: decorator is the skin, strategy the guts.

answers.body: Decorator and Strategy are identical; the names are synonyms for exchanging an algorithm at run time.
answers.comment: L6, slide 38: They are two alternative ways of changing an object, not synonyms.

name: In the shaking-molecule model a <TT>Residue</TT> references its atoms. The Strategy design gives <TT>Atom</TT> an exchangeable <TT>AtomPositionStrategy</TT> (<TT>AllInMemStrategy</TT>, <TT>BufferedStrategy</TT>). The Decorator design wraps a <TT>StaticAtom</TT> in exclusive decorators <TT>AllInMemAtom</TT> or <TT>BufferedAtom</TT> (derived from <TT>DynamicAtom</TT> with <TT>firstFrame()</TT>, <TT>nextFrame()</TT>, <TT>previousFrame()</TT>). Which statements are correct?

answers.body: With Strategy, replacing the storage strategy does not affect the Residue, which always keeps referencing the same Atom object.
answers.comment: L6, slide 41: The change of the strategy does not affect the Residue.

answers.body: With Decorator, replacing <TT>BufferedAtom</TT> by <TT>AllInMemAtom</TT> changes the outermost object, so the Residue has to update its pointer.
answers.comment: L6, slide 41: In the decorator design the Residue has to update its pointers.

answers.body: With Decorator, the Residue keeps its pointer unchanged. The decorator and the decorated atom share the same interface.
answers.comment: L6, slide 41: The shared interface does not help; the outermost object is replaced, so the pointers change.

answers.body: The decorators in this design can be stacked freely in any order, like pizza toppings, so several storage kinds can combine.
answers.comment: L6, slide 40: The slide notes the adaptation that the decorators are exclusive.

answers.body: A decorator design cannot offer jumping to the N-th frame. A generic decorator interface only moves sequentially.
answers.comment: L6, slide 40: The generic interface moves sequentially, and a specific decorator (all in memory) adds jumping to the N-th position.

name: Which pairs of a Java core API element and the design pattern it exemplifies are correct?

answers.body: <TT>java.util.Comparator#compare()</TT>, passed to <TT>new TreeSet(comparator)</TT>, is a sorting strategy: Strategy.
answers.comment: L6, slide 12: The comparator is an exchangeable sorting algorithm of the set.

answers.body: <TT>java.util.Arrays#asList(T...)</TT> integrates an array into the list API, with changes written through: Adapter.
answers.comment: L6, slide 26: The array is the class we integrate into the API of lists.

answers.body: <TT>java.io.BufferedWriter</TT> adapts a Writer to a new interface that supports buffering: Adapter.
answers.comment: L6, slide 37: BufferedWriter adds buffering on top of a Writer with the same interface, which is Decorator.

answers.body: <TT>java.util.Comparator</TT> switches the behavior of a TreeSet when the set changes its internal state: State.
answers.comment: L6, slide 12: A comparator is an exchangeable sorting strategy passed in from outside, not a state of the set.

answers.body: <TT>java.util.Arrays#asList(T...)</TT> adds sorting behavior around an existing list object: Decorator.
answers.comment: L6, slide 26: It converts an array to the list interface, which is Adapter.

name: An online shop has an <TT>Order</TT>. Its <TT>computePrice()</TT> must use either a regular pricing policy or a sale pricing policy, chosen by the sales department. Its <TT>pay()</TT> and <TT>ship()</TT> behave differently while the order is New, Paid or Shipped, and the order itself updates its status. Model the problem in UML (a) with the Strategy pattern for pricing and (b) with the State pattern for the status. Show the classes, roles, key operations and who decides about the variant, and explain how the two patterns differ although their diagrams look similar. (The scenario is derived; the patterns are from the lecture.)
answer:
(a) Strategy. <<context>> Order with computePrice() aggregates exactly one <<strategy>> PricingPolicy with price(items) : Money. RegularPricing and SalePricing implement it. The client that understands the policies (the sales department's code) creates one and passes it to the order, e.g. through the constructor or setPricingPolicy; computePrice() delegates to it. The strategy handles one specific task, receives the data it needs as parameters and does not store the order, so the interface can be somewhat more complex (limited access to the context). A new policy is a new class and Order stays unchanged (open-closed).
(b) State. <<context>> Order holds a state association to the <<state>> interface OrderState with pay() and ship(); NewOrder, PaidOrder and ShippedOrder implement it. Order delegates its requests to the current state and may pass itself to it. The order or the state itself decides the successor, e.g. NewOrder.pay() calls order.setState(new PaidOrder()). Clients talk only to Order. This replaces a large conditional on a status attribute and makes the transitions explicit.
Difference. A strategy is passed in from outside, handles one task, and neither stores the context nor replaces itself. States are created by the context (or by other states), may hold the context, may replace themselves, and provide the implementation of almost everything the context does. Prefer Strategy for a policy that a client chooses; prefer State when behavior follows the object's own life-cycle.
keyPoints: Strategy: Order as context with one PricingPolicy; RegularPricing and SalePricing implement it
Strategy is chosen and passed in by a client; it handles one task and does not know the context
State: Order as context with OrderState; NewOrder, PaidOrder, ShippedOrder implement pay() and ship()
Order or state objects switch the state (setState); clients use only Order
Difference: who creates and switches the variant, context reference, scope of responsibility; similar diagrams
source: L6, slides 5-6, 13-15, 18; the order scenario is derived

name: Practical modeling: in a pizzeria system every pizza has <TT>getLabel()</TT> and <TT>getPrice()</TT>. The base pizza costs 100 and is labelled "Pizza"; cheese adds 20 and sausage adds 30 to the price and append their name to the label. Toppings can be combined freely and added to individual orders at run time. Draw a UML class diagram using the Decorator pattern, show the object structure of a pizza with cheese and sausage, and compute its label and price. Explain why the design is better than subclasses for each combination and name its liabilities.
answer:
Classes. An abstract component Pizza (or a PizzaComponent interface) with getLabel() and getPrice(); a concrete component BasePizza (label "Pizza", price 100); an abstract decorator ToppingDecorator that inherits from the component and holds exactly one component (multiplicity 1), forwarding getLabel() and getPrice() to it; concrete decorators Cheese and Sausage that call the wrapped component and add their part (Cheese: price + 20, label + ", cheese"; Sausage: price + 30, label + ", sausage").
Objects. aSausage references aCheese, which references aPizza. The price is \(30 + (20 + 100) = 150\), and the label is "Pizza, cheese, sausage" (the label order depends on the wrapping order).
Benefits. Responsibilities are attached to individual objects dynamically and can be withdrawn; one class per topping replaces a subclass for every combination (\(2^n - 1\) combinations for \(n\) toppings, e.g. \(2^3 - 1 = 7\)), so feature-laden classes high in the hierarchy are avoided and new toppings are added without touching existing classes.
Liabilities. A decorated pizza is not identical to the wrapped component object (identity checks fail), and the design creates lots of little objects.
keyPoints: Component Pizza with getLabel/getPrice; BasePizza as concrete component
Abstract decorator inherits from the component and wraps exactly one component
Cheese and Sausage decorators add to price and label after delegating
aSausage references aCheese references aPizza; price 150, label "Pizza, cheese, sausage"
Dynamic, per-object, withdrawable; avoids the \(2^n - 1\) combination subclasses
Liabilities: decorator is not identical to its component, many little objects
source: L6, slides 33-36; prices are example data, the subclass count is derived

name: A reporting module works with an interface <TT>Notifier</TT> that has <TT>send(recipient, text)</TT>. A vendor class <TT>SmsGateway</TT>, which you may not modify, offers <TT>transmit(phoneNumber, payload, priority)</TT>, and the vendor also ships subclasses such as <TT>BulkSmsGateway</TT>. Draw UML class diagrams of an object adapter and of a class adapter that make the gateway usable as a <TT>Notifier</TT>, sketch the code of <TT>send</TT> for the object adapter, and explain which variant you choose here and why. (The scenario is derived; the pattern is from the lecture.)
answer:
Object adapter. SmsNotifier implements Notifier and holds an association to an SmsGateway (the adaptee). 
void send(String recipient, String text) {
  gateway.transmit(phoneOf(recipient), text, NORMAL);
}
The adapter converts the interface (recipient and text to phone number, payload and a priority; the conversion and constant are assumptions) and re-sends the request to the adaptee.
Class adapter. SmsNotifierC inherits from both the target Notifier and the adaptee SmsGateway (multiple inheritance; in Java the target would be an interface) and implements send by calling the inherited transmit(...).
Choice. Choose the object adapter. One adapter then works with SmsGateway and all its subclasses such as BulkSmsGateway, whereas a class adapter commits to one concrete adaptee class and would need a separate adapter for each subclass. The price is that overriding vendor behavior is harder: it would require subclassing the adaptee and referring to that subclass. A class adapter fits when we need to override some adaptee behavior and want a single object without pointer indirection. An adapter only converts the interface; it does not add responsibilities (that would be Decorator).
keyPoints: Object adapter: SmsNotifier implements Notifier and holds an SmsGateway; send converts and re-sends
Class adapter: inherits from Notifier and SmsGateway; send calls the inherited transmit
Object adapter chosen: it works with the adaptee and all its subclasses
Class adapter commits to one concrete adaptee class; it can override adaptee behavior and needs no indirection
Adapter converts the interface only; adding responsibilities is Decorator
source: L6, slides 20-25; the SMS scenario is derived

name: A TV manufacturer programs every TV model separately for each kind of remote controller. Currently there are two TV models and two controller kinds (push-button and touch); a third TV model and a gesture controller are planned. The generic controller interface offers "switch to channel X", "next channel" and "volume up"; the TV's own remote-control interface may be lower-level. Model the problem with the Bridge pattern: draw a UML class diagram with the pattern roles, explain how the abstraction reaches the implementation, and count the concrete classes needed with and without Bridge after both extensions.
answer:
Roles. The abstraction RemoteController offers the generic interface (switchToChannel(x), nextChannel(), volumeUp()) and holds a reference imp to the implementor. The refined abstractions PushButtonController, TouchController and later GestureController extend the interface with their own operations (press button 1, swipe right, ...). The implementor interface TVImplementor is the TV's remote-control interface and may be lower-level than the abstraction's; the concrete implementors are TvModelX, TvModelY and later TvModelZ.
Collaboration. A controller operation such as nextChannel() is implemented by calling imp.operationImp() on the TV it is bound to, so the two hierarchies are connected only by this reference (the bridge) and can be extended independently; the binding to a TV can also be chosen or switched at run time.
Count (derived). Without Bridge every combination is a class: \(2 \times 2 = 4\) now and \(3 \times 3 = 9\) after the extensions, i.e. \(m \times n\). With Bridge, only the two hierarchies grow: \(2 + 2 = 4\) now and \(3 + 3 = 6\) concrete classes afterwards, i.e. \(m + n\), plus the abstraction and implementor interfaces. Adding a TV model touches no controller class and vice versa.
keyPoints: Abstraction RemoteController with a generic interface and a reference imp to the implementor
Refined abstractions (push-button, touch, gesture) extend the interface; concrete implementors are TV models
imp.operationImp(): the implementor interface may differ and be lower-level
The two hierarchies extend independently; the implementation can be switched at run time
Count: \(m \times n\) combination classes without Bridge, \(m + n\) with Bridge (4 growing to 9 versus 4 growing to 6)
source: L6, slides 27-30; the class counts are derived
